interactions.summary: Jiang formalizes the logical model behind the moon debate by translating darkness into hollowness, density, and light transmission, then names the whole move as analysis by categorization.

The reader continues Beatrice’s rebuttal: the heavens display different powers, rarity cannot explain the visible differences, and the eclipse thought experiment is introduced to defeat the hollow-moon option.

Jiang frames the scene as a scientific argument taking place in heaven and paraphrases Beatrice’s rebuttal as a refusal to let one logical principle explain all celestial variety, before reducing the alternatives to two material hypotheses that she will destroy.

claims.claim: Jiang says the logical explanation assumes dark regions are hollow or cavity-like, allowing light to pass through, while dense regions reflect it back.
Jiang explicitly names this hollow-versus-dense explanation as the product of logic and categorization, while also saying Dante is about to show why it fails.
Jiang highlights the scene’s novelty by saying the Divine Comedy stages a scientific debate in heaven and therefore makes the nature of science itself part of the poem’s argument.
The quoted passage argues that different stars show different powers, so one single principle such as rarity and density cannot account for all celestial variation.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted literary material read aloud on 2026-06-15.

claims.claim: Jiang paraphrases Beatrice as saying that if one reducible logic governed all the stars, every star would be lit by the same logic, but heavenly variation shows another force is at work.
The quoted text reduces the rarity thesis to two options: either the moon lacks matter through and through in some parts, or density alternates within it the way lean and fat alternate in a body.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted literary material read aloud on 2026-06-15.

claims.claim: Jiang translates Beatrice’s dilemma into two material hypotheses for the class: the moon has hollow sections, or it contains deep cavities, and he says Beatrice will now refute both.
The eclipse argument says that if the moon were truly hollow in the relevant way, sunlight would show through it during an eclipse, and because that does not happen the first hypothesis collapses.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted literary reasoning read aloud on 2026-06-15.

signature_moments.moment: Paradiso is presented as heaven hosting an argument about what science can and cannot do.
signature_moments.source_phrase: they're in heaven and they're having a scientific debate
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the packet’s most memorable frame: Dante does not abandon inquiry in heaven, he radicalizes it.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats celestial difference as proof that one flattening logic cannot govern the whole universe.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's another force that's at work
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This keeps the packet from becoming only about lunar physics; it widens into a claim about plurality in the structure of reality.

signature_moments.moment: The eclipse becomes the surgical test that destroys the hollow-moon explanation.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if I annul that too then your opinion surely is confused
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures Beatrice using empirical-style reasoning inside a poem to dismantle the class’s first logical answer.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang’s framing for the moon passage, where metaphysical ascent includes an argument about scientific explanation.
Appears in the reading as the basis for different celestial powers, against any single density-based explanation.
The thought experiment Beatrice uses to show that a truly hollow moon would let sunlight show through during an eclipse.

chronology_notes.note: This packet continues the same June 15 close reading and deepens the logical refutation sequence; it does not mark a dated change relative to other sources.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang’s paraphrase of the star passage is loose and pedagogical rather than textually exact, so the 'another force' language should be treated as his interpretive gloss, not Dante’s literal wording.
